history.content: What do you need to know before starting a small claims case?

Before starting a small claims case, you need to know where the person or business you think owes you money is located so you can put that address on the court forms. You also need to have a legal reason for suing, and figure out who you should sue and how to find them. Some kinds of cases have special rules you must follow. Additionally, you should consider whether you have proof of your claim and if you will be able to obtain it in time for your court hearing. If the person you want to sue lives outside California, there may be special rules and considerations.
What is a small claims court?

The Small Claims Court is a specialized court designed to resolve disputes quickly and affordably. Cases heard in Small Claims involve damages of $10,000 or less. This process is accessible and efficient, with simple and informal rules in place. 
Attorneys are not permitted to represent parties in Small Claims Court. However, you can seek advice from a lawyer before your court appearance. The hearing itself is informal, and the rules are straightforward. Overall, Small Claims Court aims to settle disputes fairly, quickly, and at a low cost.
Can I use a mediator instead?

Yes, an alternative to formal litigation in the court is the use of a mediator. A mediator is an impartial, neutral intermediary whose role is to facilitate discussions between the parties in order to help them reach an agreement. The mediator does not impose a settlement but assists the parties in exploring different settlement options. Generally, the mediator does not communicate with the court except to file the parties’ settlement agreement.
You can mediate your case either before or after a small claims case has been filed. If you mediate before filing a case and reach an agreement, there will be no need to file a small claims case. If a case has already been filed, the agreement reached during mediation can be entered into the court record without requiring a court appearance. You may also have the opportunity to mediate your case on the day of the hearing at the courthouse.
Is the mediator a public employee?
What is the maximum amount for a claim in small claims court?

The maximum amount you can dispute is $10,000 if you are an individual. If you are filing on behalf of a business, the limit for your claim is $5,000. You can file as many claims as you want in small claims court, but each claim must not exceed $2,500. However, you are limited to two claims of up to $5,000 each during the calendar year.
Can I file an appeal if I lose the case?
The judge’s decision is final, so you may not appeal your own claim. However, you can appeal if you are sued, or the other side sues you back, and you lose.
Do you have any other questions that I can assist?
What are the differences between small claims cases and limited civil cases?

The filing fees for small claims are lower, typically up to $100. In contrast, limited civil cases have higher starting fees, beginning at $225.
Small claims and limited civil cases differ in several important ways. The small claims process is informal and more straightforward, whereas limited civil cases require adherence to all the rules and procedures of regular civil litigation, which can be complicated and time-consuming.
 Cases in small claims court are usually resolved more quickly, typically within three months. Limited civil cases, however, can take a year or longer to conclude.
In small claims, a plaintiff cannot appeal the decision. However, in limited civil cases, either party has the right to appeal.
 In small claims court, a person cannot file more than two suits in a calendar year for amounts exceeding $2,500. There is no such limit in limited civil cases.
Small claims are generally more accessible and faster, while limited civil cases involve more complexity and a longer timeframe.

Do I need a safe room? What is a safe room?

A safe room, as defined by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), is a room - preferably below ground - in which people can take shelter from a tornado. If such a room is below ground, it may not be the safest choice if told to stay at home and shelter-in-place during a weapons of mass destruction event due to the possibility that some contaminants may seep into rooms below ground level. For this reason, the Red Cross recommends and endorses having a safe room in areas where tornadoes are a threat.

Any mistake, even a small one, can mean that your case is dismissed, you lose, or in some situations even that you may have to pay for the other side’s lawyers' fees and costs.
Where you can get legal help or information that you will need
Sometimes, if you start or respond to a case on your own, you may find later in your case you do not know what to do next.  You may be able to find a lawyer who can help you just with the parts that are more challenging for you to do on your own. Your court's Self-Help Center may have resources for you.
If you decide not to get a lawyer or you cannot find one, you may find some helpful information on the Sacramento Law Library's Legal Research page. The library also has a guide with the steps you'll have to follow to start a civil case or respond to a lawsuit. Much of the information applies to every county in California. Or contact your local law library for help in your county.
